title: Why the Man at Bethesda Stayed Sick for 38 Years
paragraphs: Why the Man at Bethesda Stayed Sick for 38 Years
Jerusalem was loud that morning.
Feet scraping stone. Merchants shouting. Animals moving through narrow streets. Religious men adjusting robes. Pilgrims carrying burdens nobody could see.
And beside the Sheep Gate… there was a place people tried not to stare at too long.
Bethesda.
The House of Mercy.
In Hebrew, בית חסדא (Beit Chesda). A name filled with compassion. A location filled with suffering.
And sometimes that is exactly what life feels like.
A place named mercy… where pain still lives.
John 5 opens with one of the most haunting scenes in all of Scripture. Not because of demons. Not because of violence. Not because of judgment.
Because of hopelessness.
“Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades. In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.” — John 5:2–3
A multitude.
Not one hurting person. Thousands. Bodies broken. Dreams buried. Eyes watching water. Souls waiting for movement.
But hidden among the crowd was one man whose story feels terrifyingly familiar.
“One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.” — John 5:5
Thirty-eight years.
Almost four decades.

Long enough for people to stop asking what happened. Long enough for disappointment to become identity. Long enough for suffering to stop feeling temporary. Long enough to forget what hope even sounded like.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because some people reading this are not physically paralyzed. But emotionally? Spiritually? Mentally?
You have been stuck for years.
Stuck in addiction. Stuck in compromise. Stuck in depression. Stuck in pornography. Stuck in shame. Stuck in fear. Stuck in cycles nobody around you even knows about.
Still smiling online. Still posting Bible verses. Still attending church. Still pretending.
But inside? You have been lying beside your own Bethesda for years.
And the terrifying part is this: You can become so familiar with dysfunction that healing starts to feel uncomfortable.
Most people assume the man stayed sick because he was unlucky. But Jesus exposes something much deeper.
“When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, ‘Do you want to be healed?’” — John 5:6
At first, the question sounds almost offensive.
Of course he wants healing. Why else would he be there?
But Jesus never asks unnecessary questions.
The Greek wording here is powerful.
θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; (“Theleis hygiēs genesthai?”)
Literally: “Do you truly desire to become whole?”
Not merely cured. Whole.
Because healing changes more than pain. Healing changes identity. Responsibility. Lifestyle. Relationships. Habits. Dependence. Excuses.
And some people want relief without transformation.
That question still echoes today.
Do you want freedom? Or have you become emotionally attached to your chains?
Do you want Christ? Or just temporary comfort?
Do you want healing? Or do you only want sympathy?
The man’s response is heartbreaking.
“The sick man answered him, ‘Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.’” — John 5:7
Notice something carefully.
Jesus asked about healing. The man answered with excuses.
For 38 years he had mastered the language of limitation.
“No one helps me.” “Someone always gets there first.” “My situation is unfair.” “I tried before.”
And to be fair… some of it was true.
Trauma was real. Pain was real. Abandonment was real.
But somewhere along the way, his explanation became his prison.
And millions of people are doing the same thing right now.
Still rehearsing what happened. Still replaying betrayal. Still reliving childhood wounds. Still using past pain to explain present paralysis.
At some point, the pain that happened to you becomes the identity you protect.
And this is where the Gospel becomes confrontational.
Because Jesus is compassionate enough to understand your suffering… but holy enough to refuse to let you live chained to it forever.
Jesus does not negotiate with paralysis. He commands movement.
“Jesus said to him, ‘Get up, take up your bed, and walk.’” — John 5:8
In Greek: Ἔγειρε, ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ περιπάτει. (Egeire, aron ton krabatton sou kai peripatei.)
“Rise. Carry what once carried you. Walk continuously.”
This was not merely physical healing. This was spiritual resurrection language.
The same Jesus who would later walk out of a tomb first walked into Bethesda.
And what happened next is almost unbelievable.
“And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked.” — John 5:9
At once.
Not gradually. Not eventually. Not after another 38 years.
One encounter with Jesus accomplished what decades of striving could not.
Because Christ does not merely improve broken people. He resurrects dead places.
But the deeper question still remains.
Why did the man stay sick for 38 years?
The answer is painful.
Because proximity to healing is not the same as surrendering to Jesus.
He spent decades near a pool. But one moment near Christ changed everything.
And this is where many believers silently struggle.
You can spend years around church culture while remaining spiritually paralyzed.
Near worship. Near sermons. Near Scripture. Near Christian content. Near ministry.
But still not surrendered.
Still hiding. Still resisting. Still carrying secret sin. Still delaying obedience. Still blaming others. Still waiting for someone else to carry you.
Bethesda was filled with people waiting for movement in the water. Meanwhile, the Living Water was standing in front of them.
And some people are still missing Jesus while sitting inside religious spaces.
That is the terrifying tragedy of familiarity.
You can become so used to spiritual language that you stop recognizing the voice of God.
The pool itself reveals something heartbreaking about human nature.
People believed healing came through being first. Competition. Desperation. Survival.
Whoever got there first won. Everybody else stayed broken.
That sounds a lot like modern culture.
Fight harder. Climb faster. Perform better. Curate the perfect image. Hide weakness. Outrun everybody.
But the Kingdom of God does not operate through scrambling. Grace is not awarded to the fastest person in the room.
The crippled man could never win that race.
Which is exactly why Jesus came directly to him.
Because grace walks toward people who cannot save themselves.
And maybe this is the part somebody desperately needs to hear.
Jesus was not disgusted by the man’s weakness.
He walked straight toward it.
Toward the smell. Toward the disappointment. Toward the hopelessness. Toward the years wasted. Toward the bitterness. Toward the excuses. Toward the broken identity.
Toward him.
Toward you.

Somebody reading this has secretly believed they waited too long. That God is done with them. That too many years were wasted. That their compromise ruined their future. That their addiction became permanent. That their hidden sin disqualified them.
But Bethesda proves something unforgettable.
Jesus still walks into places filled with broken people.
And He still asks impossible questions.
“Do you want to be made whole?”
Not perform better. Not look more religious. Not fake holiness.
Whole.
The story becomes even more intense later.
Jesus finds the healed man again in the temple and says:
“See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.” — John 5:14
Modern culture hates verses like this.
But Jesus lovingly reveals a truth many avoid: Some suffering is connected to sinful living.
Not all sickness. Scripture never teaches that every illness is personal punishment.
But Jesus clearly warns that spiritual destruction can become worse than physical suffering.
Why?
Because eternity is longer than 38 years.
This is why the Gospel is not merely self-improvement. It is rescue.
The deepest paralysis in this story was never the man’s legs. It was humanity’s separation from God.
And Jesus came to carry what we never could.
Isaiah prophesied this centuries earlier:
“Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows.” — Isaiah 53:4
In Hebrew: אָכֵן חֳלָיֵנוּ הוּא נָשָׂא (Akhen cholayenu hu nasa)
“Surely our sicknesses He carried.”
The cross was not symbolic. It was substitution.
Jesus entered humanity’s Bethesda. He stepped into our contamination. He carried our sin. He bore wrath we deserved. He conquered death itself.
And three days later, the stone moved. Not so Jesus could get out. But so humanity could finally see hope had risen.
The man at Bethesda could not heal himself. Neither can we.
Religion cannot save you. Performance cannot save you. Internet motivation cannot save you. Your own strength cannot save you.
Only Christ.
Only the crucified and risen Son of God.
And maybe the most terrifying possibility is this: Some people have been spiritually sick for so long they no longer remember who they were before the paralysis.
But Jesus remembers.
He remembers the version of you buried beneath shame. Beneath addiction. Beneath trauma. Beneath compromise. Beneath secret sin. Beneath exhaustion.
And He still calls your name.
This is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not God humiliating you. It is God refusing to let destruction keep devouring you.
The Greek word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a complete change of mind leading to a transformed life. Not temporary guilt. Transformation.
Jesus did not die so people could remain chained while calling themselves Christians.
He died to make dead people alive.
And somebody reading this knows the Holy Spirit is exposing something hidden right now.
The secret compromise. The private addiction. The bitterness. The sexual sin. The pride. The fake image. The exhaustion. The numbness.
You have sat beside your Bethesda long enough.
Christ is calling you to rise.
Not tomorrow. Not when life feels easier. Now.
And yes… it may cost you.
Healing often requires leaving behind the identity built around brokenness.
Some people know how to survive dysfunction better than they know how to live free.
But freedom in Christ is worth the discomfort.
Because eventually every false refuge collapses. Every distraction fades. Every hidden sin surfaces. Every earthly identity dies.
But Jesus remains.
The man at Bethesda probably woke up that morning expecting another disappointing day.
Instead, he encountered the Son of God.
And that is the terrifying beauty of grace.
One encounter with Jesus can interrupt decades of bondage.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some people were never waiting for healing. They were waiting for permission to stay broken.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Nanatiling May Sakit ang Lalaking Nasa Bethesda sa Loob ng 38 Taon
Maingay ang Jerusalem noong araw na iyon.

Tunog ng mga yabag sa bato. Sigawan ng mga nagtitinda. Paggalaw ng mga hayop sa makikitid na daan. Mga relihiyosong lider na abala sa kanilang ritwal. Mga taong may pasan-pasang problema na hindi nakikita ng iba.
At sa tabi ng Sheep Gate… may lugar na halos ayaw tingnan ng mga tao.
Bethesda.
“Bahay ng Habag.”
Sa Aramaic at Hebrew: בית חסדא (Beit Chesda)
Nakakagulat.
Lugar na ang pangalan ay habag… pero puno ng paghihirap.
At minsan, ganiyan ang pakiramdam ng buhay.
Parang nasa lugar kang tinatawag na “biyaya”… pero sugatan ka pa rin.
Sa Juan 5, isa ito sa pinakaemosyonal at pinaka-mabigat na tagpo sa buong Biblia. Hindi dahil may demonyo. Hindi dahil may digmaan. Hindi dahil may paghuhukom.
Kundi dahil may kawalan ng pag-asa.

“May isang lawa sa Jerusalem na malapit sa Pintuan ng mga Tupa, na sa wikang Aramaic ay tinatawag na Bethesda. Ito ay may limang silungan. Dito nakahiga ang maraming maysakit—mga bulag, pilay, at paralitiko.” — Juan 5:2–3
Marami.
Hindi lang isang taong sugatan. Kundi napakarami.
Mga katawan na wasak. Mga pangarap na matagal nang namatay. Mga matang nakatingin sa tubig. Mga pusong naghihintay ng himala.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon… may isang lalaking parang salamin ng maraming tao ngayon.
“May isang lalaki roon na tatlumpu’t walong taon nang may sakit.” — Juan 5:5
Tatlumput walong taon.
Halos apat na dekada.

Sobrang tagal para mawalan ng pag-asa. Sobrang tagal para masanay sa sakit. Sobrang tagal para isipin na baka hindi na magbabago ang buhay. Sobrang tagal para maging parte na ng pagkatao mo ang iyong pagkawasak.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit sobrang tumatama ang kwentong ito.
Kasi may mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na hindi man paralitiko sa katawan… pero sa loob?
Pagod na.

Paralisado sa takot. Paralisado sa kasalanan. Paralisado sa trauma. Paralisado sa depresyon. Paralisado sa pornograpiya. Paralisado sa guilt. Paralisado sa lihim na kasalanang walang ibang nakakaalam.
Ngumingiti online. Nagpo-post ng Bible verse. Uma-attend ng church.
Pero sa totoo lang? Matagal ka nang nakahiga sa sarili mong Bethesda.
At ang nakakatakot?
Kapag sobrang tagal mo nang sugatan… minsan nagiging komportable ka na sa pagkasira.
Akala ng karamihan kaya nanatiling may sakit ang lalaki ay dahil malas siya.
Pero may mas malalim na inilalantad si Jesus.
“Nang makita siya ni Jesus na nakahiga roon at malaman na matagal na siyang may sakit, sinabi Niya sa kanya, ‘Gusto mo bang gumaling?’” — Juan 5:6
Parang kakaiba ang tanong.
Siyempre gusto niyang gumaling.
Pero si Jesus hindi nagtatanong nang walang dahilan.
Sa Greek: θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; (Theleis hygiēs genesthai?)
Ibig sabihin: “Talaga bang gusto mong maging buo?”
Hindi lang gumaling. Maging buo.
Kasi ang tunay na pagpapagaling hindi lang inaalis ang sakit. Binabago nito ang pagkatao.
At minsan… gusto natin ng ginhawa pero ayaw natin ng transformation.
Gusto natin ng blessing pero ayaw natin ng surrender.
Gusto natin ng himala pero ayaw natin bitawan ang kasalanan.
Kaya hanggang ngayon, parang bumubulong pa rin ang tanong ni Jesus.
Gusto mo bang maging malaya? O nasanay ka na sa tanikala mo?
Gusto mo ba talaga si Cristo? O gusto mo lang ng pansamantalang comfort?
Ang sagot ng lalaki ay sobrang lungkot.
“Ginoo, wala pong maglalagay sa akin sa tubig kapag gumalaw ito. At habang papunta ako, may nauuna na sa akin.” — Juan 5:7
Pansinin mo ito.
Tinanong siya ni Jesus tungkol sa healing. Ang isinagot niya… dahilan.
Sa loob ng 38 taon, nasanay siyang ipaliwanag kung bakit hindi siya makabangon.
“Walang tumutulong sa akin.” “Laging may nauuna.” “Hindi patas ang buhay.” “Nasubukan ko na dati.”
At oo… may katotohanan doon.
Totoo ang sakit. Totoo ang trauma. Totoo ang abandonment.
Pero minsan, ang dahilan na dati mong sugat… nagiging kulungan mo na.
At milyon-milyong tao ngayon ang ganito.
Paulit-ulit na nire-replay ang betrayal. Paulit-ulit na dinadala ang trauma. Paulit-ulit na ginagamit ang nakaraan para ipaliwanag kung bakit hindi sila makausad.
At dito nagiging confrontational ang Gospel.
Kasi naiintindihan ni Jesus ang sakit mo… pero mahal ka Niya nang sobra para hayaan kang manatiling nakakadena habambuhay.
Hindi nakikipag-negotiate si Jesus sa paralysis. Inuutusan Niya itong tumayo.
“Tumayo ka. Buhatin mo ang iyong higaan at lumakad ka.” — Juan 5:8
Sa Greek: Ἔγειρε, ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ περιπάτει. (Egeire, aron ton krabatton sou kai peripatei.)
“Bumangon. Buhatin mo ang bagay na dating bumubuhat sa’yo. At patuloy kang lumakad.”
Hindi lang ito physical healing. Parang resurrection language ito.
Ang parehong Jesus na lalabas mula sa libingan… unang pumasok sa Bethesda.
At biglang nangyari ang imposible.
“Agad na gumaling ang lalaki; binuhat niya ang kanyang higaan at lumakad.” — Juan 5:9
Agad.
Hindi unti-unti. Hindi pagkatapos ng ilang taon. Hindi matapos ang isa pang 38 years.
Isang encounter kay Jesus ang nagawa ang hindi kayang gawin ng dekada ng paghihintay.
Kasi si Cristo hindi lang nag-aayos ng sirang tao. Binubuhay Niya ang patay na bahagi ng puso.
Pero bakit nga ba nanatiling may sakit ang lalaki sa loob ng 38 taon?
Masakit ang sagot.
Dahil ang pagiging malapit sa himala ay hindi awtomatikong surrender kay Jesus.
Matagal siyang malapit sa tubig. Pero isang sandali malapit kay Cristo ang tunay na nagbago sa kanya.
At maraming tao ngayon ang ganito rin.
Matagal nang nasa church. Malapit sa worship. Malapit sa preaching. Malapit sa Christian content.
Pero hindi pa rin surrendered.
May lihim pa ring kasalanan. May tinatagong compromise. May pride. May bitterness. May double life.
Ang Bethesda puno ng taong naghihintay sa paggalaw ng tubig. Habang ang Living Water mismo ay nasa harapan nila.
At hanggang ngayon, may mga taong nasa loob ng religion pero nami-miss pa rin si Jesus.
Iyon ang delikado sa pagiging familiar.
Kapag nasanay ka sa spiritual language… minsan hindi mo na naririnig ang tunay na boses ng Diyos.
Ang sistema sa Bethesda ay parang mundo ngayon.
Paunahan. Palakasan. Pagandahan ng image. Pagalingan magtago.
Pero ang Kaharian ng Diyos hindi gumagalaw sa competition.
Ang biyaya hindi para sa pinakamabilis.
Kaya nga direktang nilapitan ni Jesus ang lalaking hindi kayang manalo.
Dahil ang grace lumalapit sa taong hindi kayang iligtas ang sarili.
At baka ito ang kailangang marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Hindi nandidiri si Jesus sa kahinaan mo.
Nilapitan ka Niya.
Nilapitan Niya ang trauma. Nilapitan Niya ang hiya. Nilapitan Niya ang pagkatalo. Nilapitan Niya ang addiction. Nilapitan Niya ang pagkasira.
Nilapitan ka Niya.
May nagbabasa nito ngayon na iniisip na baka huli na ang lahat. Na baka sawang-sawa na ang Diyos. Na baka hindi ka na kayang baguhin. Na baka permanenteng bahagi mo na ang kasalanan.
Pero pinapatunayan ng Bethesda ang isang bagay.
Patuloy pa ring pumapasok si Jesus sa lugar ng mga wasak.
At patuloy pa rin Siyang nagtatanong:
“Gusto mo bang maging buo?”
Hindi magmukhang banal. Hindi magpanggap. Hindi mag-perform.
Maging buo.
Kalaunan, nakita ulit ni Jesus ang lalaki sa templo. At sinabi Niya:
“Tingnan mo, magaling ka na. Huwag ka nang magkasala upang hindi ka mapahamak nang higit pa.” — Juan 5:14
Ayaw marinig ng modernong mundo ang mga ganitong salita.
Pero ipinapakita ni Jesus ang isang katotohanan: May mga pagkawasak na konektado sa kasalanan.
Hindi lahat ng sakit ay parusa. Hindi iyan ang itinuturo ng Biblia.
Pero malinaw na may babala si Jesus.
Bakit?
Dahil mas mahaba ang eternity kaysa 38 years.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hindi lang self-improvement ang Gospel. Ito ay rescue.
Ang pinakamalalim na paralysis sa kwentong ito ay hindi ang mga paa ng lalaki. Kundi ang pagkakahiwalay ng tao sa Diyos.
At si Jesus ang dumating para pasanin ang hindi natin kayang dalhin.
Sabi sa Isaias 53:4:
“Tunay na dinala niya ang ating mga karamdaman at pinasan ang ating mga kapighatian.”
Sa Hebrew: אָכֵן חֳלָיֵנוּ הוּא נָשָׂא (Akhen cholayenu hu nasa)
“Ang ating sakit ay Kanyang pinasan.”
Hindi simbolo ang krus. Ito ay substitution.
Pumasok si Jesus sa Bethesda ng sangkatauhan. Dinala Niya ang ating kasalanan. Pinasan Niya ang dapat na parusa natin. Tinalo Niya ang kamatayan.
At makalipas ang tatlong araw… gumulong ang bato.
Hindi para makalabas si Jesus. Kundi para makita ng mundo na nabuhay na muli ang pag-asa.
Hindi kayang pagalingin ng lalaki ang sarili niya. At ganoon din tayo.
Hindi ka kayang iligtas ng religion. Hindi ka kayang baguhin ng motivational videos. Hindi sapat ang sarili mong lakas.
Si Cristo lang.
At baka ang pinaka-mapanganib na bagay ay ito:
Kapag sobrang tagal mo nang sugatan… nakakalimutan mo na kung sino ka bago ka nasira.
Pero hindi nakakalimot si Jesus.
Naaalala Niya ang totoong ikaw. Ang ikaw bago nilamon ng shame. Bago nilamon ng addiction. Bago nilamon ng trauma. Bago nilamon ng compromise.
At tinatawag ka pa rin Niya.
Kaya mahalaga ang repentance.
Ang repentance hindi pamamahiya ng Diyos. Ito ay pagligtas Niya sa’yo mula sa destruction.
Sa Greek, ang repentance ay μετάνοια (metanoia).
Ibig sabihin: “Pagbabago ng isip na humahantong sa transformed life.”
Hindi pansamantalang guilt. Transformation.
Hindi namatay si Jesus para manatiling nakakadena ang tao habang tinatawag ang sarili nilang Kristiyano.
Namatay Siya para buhayin ang mga espirituwal na patay.
At may taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam mong kinakausap ka ng Holy Spirit.
Yung lihim na kasalanan. Yung compromise. Yung double life. Yung pagod. Yung numbness. Yung pagtatago.
Matagal ka nang nakahiga sa Bethesda.
Tinatawag ka ni Cristo para bumangon.
Hindi bukas. Hindi kapag okay na lahat. Ngayon.
Oo, mahirap.
Kasi minsan mas sanay ang tao sa dysfunction kaysa freedom.
Pero walang katulad ang kalayaan kay Cristo.
Dahil darating ang araw na lahat ng fake comfort mawawala. Lahat ng distraction matatapos. Lahat ng lihim mabubunyag.
Pero si Jesus mananatili.
Malamang ordinaryong araw lang ang inaasahan ng lalaki sa Bethesda.
Hindi niya alam na makakaharap niya ang Anak ng Diyos.
At iyon ang nakakatindig-balahibong kagandahan ng grace.
Isang encounter kay Jesus kayang putulin ang dekadang pagkakakulong.
Maging totoo ka. Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
May mga taong hindi talaga naghihintay ng healing. Naghihintay lang sila ng dahilan para manatiling wasak.
